q-ap-passive.label: Active to passive
q-ap-passive.summary: The object becomes the subject; the verb becomes a form of be + past participle in the same tense; the old subject follows 'by'.

q-ap-active.label: Passive to active
q-ap-active.summary: Undo the passive: the 'by' agent becomes the subject and the verb returns to its active form in the same tense.

q-ap-imperative.label: Passive of a command, request or piece of advice
q-ap-imperative.summary: A command with an object becomes 'Let + object + be + V3'; a command with no object becomes 'You are ordered/requested to + V1'; a piece of moral advice becomes 'Object + should + be + V3'.

q-ap-haveto.label: Passive of 'have/has/had to'
q-ap-haveto.summary: 'Subject + have/has/had + to + V1 + object' becomes 'Object + have/has/had + to + be + V3 + by + subject' — the 'to' stays, and only the verb after it turns into be + past participle.

q-ap-causative.label: Let/bid/help/make take 'to' only in the passive
q-ap-causative.summary: Let, bid, help and make are followed by a bare infinitive in the active voice but by 'to + V1' once the sentence is turned passive.

rules.text: Keep the tense: the passive of an active verb in tense T is be (in tense T) + past participle. Present perfect continuous 'have been ignoring' becomes 'has been being ignored'; simple past 'did disregard' becomes 'were disregarded'.
rules.ok: They have been ignoring the records -> The records have been being ignored by them.
rules.bad: The records had been ignored by them (a different tense).

rules.text: A modal stays unchanged: can + base becomes can + be + past participle. Do not change can to could, or add 'being'.
rules.ok: Citizens can access stamps -> Stamps can be accessed.

rules.text: In a question, 'did + base verb' becomes 'was / were + past participle': Why did the editor disregard the irregularities? -> Why were the irregularities disregarded by the editor? The tense is past, so was / were, not have been or are being.
rules.ok: Why were the irregularities disregarded by the editor?
rules.bad: Why are the irregularities being disregarded by the editor?

rules.text: To go back to active, the agent after 'by' becomes the subject, and the verb takes the tense of the passive's 'be'. 'Was being reported' becomes 'were reporting'; 'is delivered' becomes 'delivers'. If there is no agent, use someone / people.
rules.ok: It was being reported by several sources -> Several sources were reporting.
rules.bad: Several sources reported (the continuous aspect is lost).

rules.text: Do not choose a new subject from another noun in the sentence. The reception desk is where the parcel is delivered, not the doer; the unnamed doer becomes 'someone'.
rules.ok: The parcel is delivered to the reception desk -> Someone delivers the parcel to the reception desk.
rules.bad: The reception desk delivers the parcel.

rules.text: A command naming its object becomes 'Let + object + be + V3' (Shut the door -> Let the door be shut). A command with no object becomes 'You are ordered/requested/forbidden + to + V1' (Go away -> You are ordered to go away). A sentence giving moral advice becomes 'Object + should + be + V3' (Help the poor -> The poor should be helped).
rules.ok: Shut the door. -> Let the door be shut.
rules.bad: Shut the door. -> You are shut the door.

rules.text: 'Have/has/had + to + V1' keeps 'to' unchanged in the passive: only the main verb after it turns into be + past participle. 'I have to finish this work' becomes 'This work has to be finished by me', not 'This work is finished by me' and not 'This work have to finished by me'.
rules.ok: You have to choose a dress. -> A dress has to be chosen by you.
rules.bad: You have to choose a dress. -> A dress is chosen by you.

rules.text: Let, bid, help and make take a bare infinitive (no 'to') in the active voice, but the same verb takes 'to + V1' once the sentence is made passive. 'He made me wash the clothes' becomes 'I was made to wash the clothes by him', not 'I was made wash the clothes'.
rules.ok: He made me wash the clothes. -> I was made to wash the clothes by him.
rules.bad: He made me wash the clothes. -> I was made wash the clothes by him.

q-ap-passive.cue: 'Change the following from active to passive'.
q-ap-passive.standard: Find the tense and object. Put the object first, then be (in the same tense) + past participle, then 'by' + the old subject.
q-ap-passive.fast: Check the auxiliary only: has been / was / can be, and see which option matches the original tense.
q-ap-passive.eliminate: Drop options whose tense is different from the active sentence, and options with could/being added.
traps: A neat option that changes the tense (had been ignored).
Using have been / are being for a past question.

q-ap-active.cue: 'Convert the sentence from passive to active'.
q-ap-active.standard: Make the 'by' agent the subject (someone if none), keep the object, and restore the tense of the passive's be.
q-ap-active.fast: Match the tense word: was being = were / was ...ing.
q-ap-active.eliminate: Drop options that change the tense or choose a wrong subject.
traps: Using a simple past instead of the continuous.
Choosing the destination noun as the new subject.

q-ap-imperative.cue: A sentence giving an order, a request or a piece of advice, with no stated subject (or 'you' understood).
q-ap-imperative.standard: Decide which of the three patterns it is: a command with an object ('Let + object + be + V3'), a command with none ('You are ordered/requested to + V1'), or advice ('Object + should + be + V3').
q-ap-imperative.fast: An object right after the verb -> 'Let' + that object + 'be' + V3. No object -> 'You are ordered/requested to' + the base verb.
q-ap-imperative.eliminate: Drop options that put 'to' after 'Let', or that keep the command in its active imperative form.
traps: 'Let the door be shutted' — the past participle of an irregular verb is 'shut', not 'shutted'.
Swapping 'should be' for 'must be' changes a piece of advice into an obligation.

q-ap-haveto.cue: 'have to', 'has to' or 'had to' followed by a base verb and an object.
q-ap-haveto.standard: Move the object to the front, keep 'have/has/had to' exactly as it is, and change only the verb after 'to' into 'be + past participle'.
q-ap-haveto.fast: has to + V1 -> has to be + V3; the 'to' never disappears and never doubles.
q-ap-haveto.eliminate: Drop any option that drops 'to', or that turns 'have to' itself into a passive form.
traps: Treating 'have to' like an ordinary modal and writing 'can be' style passives that lose the obligation.
Forgetting the 'be' and writing 'has to finished'.

q-ap-causative.cue: let, bid, help or make followed directly by a base verb with no 'to' in an active sentence that is being turned passive.
q-ap-causative.standard: Keep the causative verb's own tense, but insert 'to' before the base verb that follows it once the sentence becomes passive.
q-ap-causative.fast: made/bid/helped + V1 (active) -> was made/bidden/helped + to + V1 (passive).
q-ap-causative.eliminate: Drop any passive option that keeps the bare infinitive with no 'to'.
traps: Copying the active sentence's bare infinitive straight into the passive, where 'to' is required.

pyqs.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
They have been ignoring preservation of the records for years.
options: Preservation of the records had been ignored by them for years.
Preservation of the records is being ignored by them for years.
Preservation of the records was being ignored by them for years.
Preservation of the records has been being ignored by them for years.
pyqs.why: The active verb is present perfect continuous (have been ignoring). Its passive is has been being ignored, the only option that keeps both the perfect and the continuous aspect.

a.note: 'Had been ignored' is past perfect, a different tense from the present perfect continuous.

b.note: 'Is being ignored' is present continuous; it loses the perfect aspect that 'for years' needs.

c.note: 'Was being ignored' is past continuous and loses the link with the present.

pyqs.caution: 'Has been being ignored' is correct but clumsy; it is the only option that keeps the original tense, which is why it is the key.

pyqs.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
It was being reported by several sources that the mission had been compromised internally.
options: Several sources were reporting that the mission had been compromised internally.
The mission was compromised, several sources reported.
The sources were reporting an internal mission compromise.
The mission had compromised several internal sources.
pyqs.why: 'It was being reported by several sources' becomes 'Several sources were reporting'; the that-clause stays unchanged.

b.note: This changes 'was being reported' to a simple past and rewrites the clause, so the tense is lost.

c.note: This reshapes the that-clause into a noun phrase and changes what was reported.

d.note: This swaps the subject and object, which reverses the meaning.

pyqs.trick: was being reported by X -> X were reporting.

pyqs.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Citizens can rarely access archived stamps without clearance.
options: Archived stamps can rarely being accessed without clearance.
Archived stamps could rarely be accessed without clearance.
Archived stamps can rarely be accessed without clearance.
Archived stamps are rarely able to be accessed without clearance.
pyqs.why: A modal stays as it is: can + be + past participle.

a.note: 'Can being accessed' is not a correct form.

b.note: 'Could' changes 'can' to a past modal, so the tense and sense shift.

d.note: 'Are rarely able to be accessed' rewrites the modal and is a clumsy paraphrase.

pyqs.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
The parcel is delivered to the reception desk every evening.
options: The reception desk delivers the parcel every evening.
Someone delivers the parcel to the reception desk every evening.
The reception desk has delivered the parcel every evening.
The parcel delivers itself to the reception desk every evening.
pyqs.why: No doer is named, so 'someone' becomes the subject, and 'is delivered' becomes 'delivers' in the same present tense.

a.note: The reception desk is the place of delivery, not the doer; this makes it the subject.

c.note: This changes the tense to the present perfect and also makes the desk the doer.

d.note: A parcel does not deliver itself; this distorts the meaning.

pyqs.caution: The original passive names no doer. 'Someone' is invented to complete the active form, which is the only option that keeps the meaning.

pyqs.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
It has been claimed that important data was being disclosed by employees within the firm.
options: Someone has claimed that employees were disclosing important data within the firm.
Important data had been disclosed by employees, it is claimed.
Employees have allegedly been disclosing important data within the firm.
The firm was allegedly disclosing employee's data.
pyqs.why: 'It has been claimed' becomes 'Someone has claimed'; 'was being disclosed by employees' becomes 'employees were disclosing'.

b.note: This stays passive and changes the tense of 'was being disclosed'.

c.note: This changes the 'has been claimed' frame into 'allegedly' and shifts the clause to present perfect continuous.

d.note: This makes the firm the doer, which reverses the meaning.

pyqs.trick: Do each clause: has been claimed -> has claimed; was being disclosed -> were disclosing.

pyqs.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Why did the editor disregard the major stylistic irregularities?
options: Why have the major stylistic irregularities been disregarded by the editor?
Why are the major stylistic irregularities being disregarded by the editor?
Why did the major stylistic irregularities be disregarded by the editor?
Why were the major stylistic irregularities disregarded by the editor?
pyqs.why: The active verb 'did disregard' is simple past, so the passive is 'were disregarded'.

a.note: 'Have been disregarded' is present perfect, a different tense.

b.note: 'Are being disregarded' is present continuous, a different tense.

c.note: 'Did ... be disregarded' is not a correct passive form.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
The committee will announce the results tomorrow.
options: The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results will announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results would be announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results are announced by the committee tomorrow.
practice.why: Future simple passive: will + be + past participle.

b.note: The 'be' is missing after 'will'.

c.note: 'Would' changes the tense of 'will'.

d.note: The present simple loses the future sense.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
The students are watching a film.
options: A film is watched by the students.
A film is being watched by the students.
A film was being watched by the students.
A film has been watched by the students.
practice.why: Present continuous passive: is / are + being + past participle.

a.note: This is the present simple passive and loses the 'watching' now.

c.note: This is past continuous.

d.note: This is present perfect.

practice.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
The bridge was built by the engineers in two years.
options: The engineers built the bridge in two years.
The engineers were building the bridge in two years.
The engineers had built the bridge in two years.
The bridge built the engineers in two years.
practice.why: Simple past passive 'was built' goes back to simple past 'built'.

b.note: This changes simple past to past continuous.

c.note: This changes simple past to past perfect.

d.note: Subject and object are swapped.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Who wrote this letter?
options: By whom was this letter written?
By whom is this letter written?
Who was this letter written?
By whom has this letter been written?
practice.why: 'Who wrote' is simple past; the passive is 'By whom was this letter written?'

b.note: Present simple loses the past tense.

c.note: 'Who' cannot replace the 'by whom' agent here.

d.note: Present perfect changes the tense.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants were being watered by the gardener.
The plants have been watered by the gardener.
practice.why: Present continuous passive keeps both the present and the continuous: is/are + being + past participle.

a.note: This is the present simple passive and loses the 'at this moment' sense of 'is watering'.

c.note: 'Were being watered' moves the sentence into the past.

d.note: 'Have been watered' is the present perfect: the action is finished, not going on.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
You must submit the form before Friday.
options: The form must be submitted before Friday.
The form must being submitted before Friday.
The form should be submitted before Friday.
The form is must submitted before Friday.
practice.why: A modal is carried over unchanged and takes be + past participle: must be submitted.

b.note: 'Must being submitted' is not a possible form; a modal takes the bare 'be'.

c.note: 'Should' weakens 'must' from an obligation to a recommendation.

d.note: 'Is must submitted' puts two verbs together with no passive form at all.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
They had completed the survey before the monsoon began.
options: The survey was completed before the monsoon began.
The survey has been completed before the monsoon began.
The survey had been completed before the monsoon began.
The survey had being completed before the monsoon began.
practice.why: Past perfect active 'had completed' becomes past perfect passive 'had been completed'; the tense must survive the change.

a.note: 'Was completed' is the simple past and loses the 'earlier than the other past event' sense that 'had' carries.

b.note: 'Has been completed' is the present perfect, which cannot sit beside the past 'began'.

d.note: 'Had being completed' is not a possible form.

practice.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
The decision was taken by the committee last week.
options: The committee took the decision last week.
The committee had taken the decision last week.
The committee takes the decision last week.
The committee was taking the decision last week.
practice.why: Simple past passive 'was taken' returns to the simple past active 'took', and the 'by' agent becomes the subject.

b.note: 'Had taken' is the past perfect, a tense the original does not have.

c.note: The present simple cannot go with 'last week'.

d.note: 'Was taking' adds a continuous aspect the original does not have.

practice.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
The streets are swept every morning.
options: The streets sweep every morning.
Someone sweeps the streets every morning.
Someone is sweeping the streets every morning.
The morning sweeps the streets.
practice.why: No doer is named, so 'someone' becomes the subject, and the present simple passive returns to the present simple active.

a.note: Streets cannot sweep; this makes the object the doer.

c.note: 'Is sweeping' adds a continuous aspect that 'are swept every morning' does not have.

d.note: 'The morning' is the time, not the doer; it is the same mistake as making the destination the subject.

practice.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
It is believed by many that the bridge is unsafe.
options: Many believe that the bridge is unsafe.
Many believed that the bridge is unsafe.
The bridge is believed unsafe by many.
Many are believing that the bridge is unsafe.
practice.why: 'It is believed by many' becomes 'Many believe'; the that-clause is left as it stands.

b.note: 'Believed' moves the sentence into the past, which the original does not.

c.note: This stays in the passive instead of turning the sentence active.

d.note: 'Are believing' is not used for a state of belief.

practice.text:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:
Why was the meeting cancelled by the secretary?
options: Why the secretary cancelled the meeting?
Why did the secretary cancel the meeting?
Why has the secretary cancelled the meeting?
Why the meeting was cancelled by the secretary?
practice.why: A passive past question becomes an active past question with 'did' and the bare verb: Why did the secretary cancel the meeting?

a.note: A question needs the auxiliary 'did' before the subject.

c.note: 'Has cancelled' is the present perfect, not the simple past of the original.

d.note: This leaves the sentence passive and also drops the question word order.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Close the window.
options: Let the window be closed.
Let the window be closing.
You are closed the window.
The window closes.
practice.why: A command naming its object becomes 'Let + object + be + V3': Let the window be closed.

b.note: 'Be closing' is not the past participle form the pattern needs.

c.note: This is not a recognised passive form.

d.note: This drops the command sense entirely and states a plain fact.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Leave the premises at once.
options: You are ordered to leave the premises at once.
Let you be left the premises at once.
The premises are ordered to leave at once.
You are ordered to left the premises at once.
practice.why: A command with no stated object becomes 'You are ordered/requested to + V1': You are ordered to leave the premises at once.

b.note: 'Let you be left' is not a recognised passive of a command with no object.

c.note: This makes the premises the one being ordered, which is not what the sentence means.

d.note: After 'to' the verb must be the bare base form 'leave', not the past form 'left'.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Respect your elders.
options: Your elders should be respected.
Let your elders be respect.
You are respected your elders.
Elders respect you.
practice.why: A sentence giving moral advice becomes 'Object + should + be + V3': Your elders should be respected.

b.note: After 'be' the verb needs its past participle form 'respected', not the base form 'respect'.

c.note: This is not a recognised passive form.

d.note: This reverses who respects whom.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
Water the plants every morning.
options: Let the plants be watered every morning.
Let the plants be water every morning.
The plants are ordering to water every morning.
Water is let to the plants every morning.
practice.why: A command naming its object becomes 'Let + object + be + V3': Let the plants be watered every morning.

b.note: After 'be' the verb needs the past participle 'watered', not the base form.

c.note: 'Are ordering' misuses the passive and is not a correct form.

d.note: This is not a recognised passive form.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
I have to submit this report by evening.
options: This report has to be submitted by evening by me.
This report is submitted by evening by me.
This report has to submitted by evening by me.
This report have to be submitted by evening by me.
practice.why: 'Have to + V1' keeps 'to' and turns only the main verb passive: has to be submitted.

b.note: This drops 'has to' entirely and loses the sense of obligation.

c.note: The 'be' is missing after 'has to'.

d.note: 'Have to' must agree with the new subject 'report', which is singular, so it should be 'has to'.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
She had to finish the project before the deadline.
options: The project had to be finished before the deadline by her.
The project had to finished before the deadline by her.
The project was finished before the deadline by her.
The project has to be finished before the deadline by her.
practice.why: 'Had to + V1' keeps 'to' and turns only the main verb passive: had to be finished.

b.note: The 'be' is missing after 'had to'.

c.note: This drops 'had to' entirely and loses the sense of obligation.

d.note: 'Has to' wrongly shifts the obligation into the present; the original is in the past, 'had to'.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
We have to inform the authorities about this matter.
options: The authorities have to be informed about this matter by us.
The authorities have to inform about this matter by us.
The authorities are informed about this matter by us.
The authorities has to be informed about this matter by us.
practice.why: 'Have to + V1' keeps 'to' and turns only the main verb passive: have to be informed.

b.note: The 'be' is missing after 'have to'.

c.note: This drops 'have to' entirely and loses the sense of obligation.

d.note: 'The authorities' is plural, so it must be 'have to', not 'has to'.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
The coach made the players run ten laps.
options: The players were made to run ten laps by the coach.
The players were made run ten laps by the coach.
The players made the coach run ten laps.
Ten laps were made by the players to run.
practice.why: 'Make' takes a bare infinitive in the active ('made ... run') but 'to + V1' in the passive: were made to run.

b.note: This keeps the bare infinitive 'run' with no 'to', which the passive of 'make' requires.

c.note: This swaps who is making whom do what.

d.note: This is not a recognised passive form.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
The officer bade the soldiers stand at ease.
options: The soldiers were bidden to stand at ease by the officer.
The soldiers were bidden stand at ease by the officer.
The officer was bidden to stand at ease by the soldiers.
Stand at ease was bidden to the soldiers.
practice.why: 'Bid' takes a bare infinitive in the active ('bade ... stand') but 'to + V1' in the passive: were bidden to stand.

b.note: This keeps the bare infinitive 'stand' with no 'to', which the passive of 'bid' requires.

c.note: This swaps who is bidding whom.

d.note: This is not a recognised passive form.

practice.text:
Change the following from active to passive:
She helped the child cross the busy road.
options: The child was helped to cross the busy road by her.
The child was helped cross the busy road by her.
The busy road was helped by the child to cross.
She was helped to cross the busy road by the child.
practice.why: 'Help' takes a bare infinitive in the active ('helped ... cross') but 'to + V1' in the passive: was helped to cross.

b.note: This keeps the bare infinitive 'cross' with no 'to', which the passive of 'help' requires.

c.note: This makes the road the one being helped, which is not the sentence's meaning.

d.note: This swaps who is helping whom.
